context_blurb:
Step outside and you stand in four great parts of Earth at once. Under your feet lie rock and soil; around you is air; rain, rivers and the sea are water; and you, the grass and the birds are alive. Scientists call these four parts Earth's spheres. They never work alone: each one keeps changing the others.

The geosphere is the solid Earth: its rock, sand and mud, down to the hot rock deep inside the planet. Soil belongs in the geosphere too, because most of it is tiny grains of weathered rock, rock that rain, ice and wind have slowly broken into bits. It also holds water, air and living things, but rock grains come first.

The hydrosphere is all of Earth's water, in every form and every place: the sea, rivers and lakes, ice and snow, clouds, the water vapour in the air, which is water as an invisible gas, and water underground. Rain that sinks into the earth gathers in the gaps between sand grains and in cracked rock, where a well can reach it. That groundwater is part of the hydrosphere: the sand and rock around it belong to the geosphere, but the water held inside them does not.

The atmosphere is the layer of gases around Earth: the air. Many people think air is mostly oxygen, the gas we breathe to stay alive, but it is not. Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of dry air and oxygen only about 21 percent, so there is nearly four times as much nitrogen as oxygen. The amount of water vapour ranges from almost none in dry air to about 4 percent in very damp air. The biosphere is all of Earth's living things, people included.

Now watch the spheres work on one another. The sea soaks up most of the sunlight that reaches Earth's surface, then hands much of that heat back to the air. Warm sea water heating the air above it is the hydrosphere at work on the atmosphere.

The air works on the sea in return. As wind blows across the sea, it drags on the surface and heaps the water up into ridges, so most waves are made by the wind: the atmosphere at work on the hydrosphere. Blow gently across a bowl of water and you can raise tiny waves of your own. The Moon does not make the waves that break on a beach; its pull makes the tides.

Living things work on rock as well. A pine tree growing from a crack in a cliff shows the biosphere and the geosphere at work on each other: its thickening roots pry the rock apart, so the crack widens year after year.

A volcano links the spheres too. Deep underground, magma, which is melted rock, holds water and other gases dissolved in it, squeezed in by great pressure. As the magma rises, the pressure drops and the gases bubble out, the way bubbles rush up in a fizzy drink the moment you open the bottle. Most of a volcano's gas is water vapour, usually 60 to 90 percent of it, with carbon dioxide next. So an eruption is the geosphere pouring water into the atmosphere.

Volcanic ash is not the soft ash of a campfire but tiny bits of broken rock and glass. Over many years that ash weathers into soil rich in the minerals plants need, so the geosphere feeds the biosphere, and that is why farms climb the sides of volcanoes that could one day erupt again.

The higher you go, the thinner the air. Near the top of the highest mountain, the air pressure, the push of the air around you, is only about a third of what it is at sea level, so each breath holds far less oxygen. That is why climbers there breathe from bottled oxygen. Many people guess that high air holds a smaller share of oxygen, but moving air keeps its gases well stirred, so even on the peak the air is still about 21 percent oxygen, as at the seashore.
